topic: Azure Cache for Redis during a flash sale — why 400,000 people opening one product page maxed out Azure SQL CPU, why adding servers made it worse, and how cache-aside with Redis makes the database answer once.

title.sub: A flash sale asks the database the same question 2,200 times a second.

stages.title: 400,000 phones, one push
stages.desc: ₹99 biryani, live at 12:00. Everybody taps at once.
stages.narration: Noon. A ninety-nine rupee biryani. Four hundred thousand people tap at once.

stages.title: Every tap asks the same question
stages.desc: "Show me biryani-99." And the API asks the database every single time.
stages.narration: Every tap asks the same question. Every time, the database answers.

stages.title: The database hits its ceiling
stages.desc: It needs 26 vCores of CPU. It has 8. Queries queue and time out.
stages.narration: It needs twenty-six vCores of CPU. It has eight. Queries start timing out.

stages.title: More servers made it worse
stages.desc: 3 instances became 8. That is 8 doors into the same database.
stages.narration: Add more servers? It gets worse. More doors into the database.

stages.title: It was the same answer
stages.desc: 2,200 times a second, the database worked out the exact same page.
stages.status: same item · same result · every time
stages.narration: The real problem? The same answer, worked out every single time.

stages.title: Keep one copy close
stages.desc: Azure Cache for Redis sits next to the API and keeps the answer in memory.
stages.narration: The fix: keep one copy close, in Azure Cache for Redis.

stages.title: First tap: read once
stages.desc: Redis has nothing yet, so one request queries Azure SQL and saves the answer.
stages.status: MISS → Azure SQL once → saved for 5 min
stages.narration: The first tap misses. One read from the database. Saved for five minutes.

stages.title: Everyone else: from memory
stages.desc: The next 2,199 taps that second never reach the database.
stages.status: HIT · under 1 ms · Azure SQL idle
stages.narration: Everyone else reads from memory. The page opens in a fifth of a second.

stages.title: Price changes? Delete the key
stages.desc: Write the database first, then delete the cached copy. The next read rebuilds it.
stages.narration: Price changes? Write the database, then delete the key. Never update it.

stages.title: Redis goes down?
stages.desc: Time out fast, fall back to the database, cap how many reads get through.
stages.status: Redis timeout 500 ms → Azure SQL, max 40 queries
stages.narration: Redis down? Time out fast, fall back, cap the reads. Still correct.

stages.title: Ask the database once
stages.desc: Redis for repeated reads. The database for the truth.
stages.narration: Redis for repeated reads. The database for the truth.

end.title: Ask the database once.
end.sub: Keep repeated reads in Azure Cache for Redis, and the truth in the database.

post.caption:
Picture a flash sale. 400,000 people tap one push notification at 12:00, and the product page takes 9 seconds to open. Nothing is down. 🍛

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY HAPPENING
Every tap asks the same question: "show me biryani-99". And every time, the API runs the same SQL query on Azure SQL. 12 ms of CPU each, 2,200 times a second: that needs about 26 vCores. The database has 8. CPU hits 100%, queries queue, and the API logs fill with Timeout expired.

THE WRONG FIX
Scale App Service from 3 instances to 8 and it gets worse. More servers = more doors into the same database.

THE REAL PROBLEM
Not traffic. Repetition. The database worked out the exact same answer 2,200 times a second.

THE FIX: CACHE-ASIDE WITH AZURE CACHE FOR REDIS
1. Ask Redis first.
2. On a miss, read the database once and save the answer for 5 minutes.
3. Everyone after that is served from memory.

ASP.NET Core, with HybridCache in front of Redis:

var page = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
    $"item:{id}",
    async ct => await catalog.GetItemPageAsync(id, ct));

HybridCache also lets only one request per server rebuild a missing key. That stops a cache stampede when a hot key expires at the peak.

PUT IN REDIS
Product details, ratings summary, category lists, sessions, rate-limit counters.

KEEP OUT OF REDIS
The price you charge at checkout, the cart, payment data, and anything that would be the only copy.

WHEN THE PRICE CHANGES
Write the database first, then DELETE the key. Never update it. Checkout always reads the price from the database.

IF REDIS GOES DOWN
500 ms timeout, fall back to the database, cap concurrent reads. Slower, still correct.

Full incident write-up, with the KQL and the code: blog.msdevbuild.com/blog/azure-cache-for-redis-flash-sale
